accuracy.reason: All nine objectives are correctly scoped to InnoDB where required. SQL-mode/CHECK behavior, explicit versus autocommit transactions, Repeatable Read versus current locking reads, bounded durability, secondary-key storage and asynchronous loss are supported by primary documentation. No false concurrency, freshness or recovery guarantee.

evidence.quote: MySQL supports other engines with different capabilities. For example, not every engine can roll back changes. The transaction and locking behavior in this deck describes InnoDB tables.

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE reads and locks records inside a transaction. Check and change the protected value before committing; an earlier unprotected check does not reserve it. Locking reads and writes use different current-data rules from snapshot reads, and locks may cover index ranges.

mechanisms.reason: Actors and state transitions are explicit from SQL client/server to engine, locks, index lookup, receive/apply and restore/replay. The price example explains snapshot persistence, while locking before checking provides a sound scarce-item pattern. Diagrams preserve engine boundaries, optional covering-index lookup and the recovery stop point.

evidence.quote: For example, your transaction reads a price of 10. Another transaction changes it to 12 and commits. A second plain SELECT in your transaction still sees 10, unless your transaction also changed that row.

Stores indexed columns plus the primary-key values used to find the complete row. A wide primary key therefore enlarges secondary entries; a compact stable key can reduce that cost, subject to workload requirements.

coherence.reason: Server role and storage-engine scope precede rules, transactions, concurrency, indexes and recovery. The final requirements method uses each earlier mechanism; all card objectives are taught without assuming product familiarity.

evidence.quote: Clarify read/write traffic, stale-read tolerance, acknowledged-write loss, write latency and downtime. Bound connection demand and transaction length, then validate recovery targets; different deployment needs may favor another database.

decisions.reason: Schema/mode verification, whole-transaction retries, primary-key width, query measurement, replica freshness, connection limits and tested recovery each connect benefit to cost. Unknown loss, downtime, traffic and latency requirements remain explicit rather than becoming universal MySQL defaults.

evidence.quote: Match candidate indexes to query filters and ordering. EXPLAIN shows the chosen query plan; measure representative data and requests. A scan can be cheaper for broad queries or small tables.
Test restoration and application usability, measuring recovery time. Untested files do not establish that the required recovery point is available.

clarity.reason: Storage engine, transaction/ACID, autocommit, snapshot, locking read, deadlock, clustered/secondary indexes and recovery modes are directly explained. The engine qualification and price example prevent the most likely incorrect generalizations; detail supports the conceptual scope.

evidence.quote: Automatically commits each successful statement as its own transaction when no explicit transaction is open. It is enabled by default. START TRANSACTION groups several statements until you issue COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

outcomes.reason: All six criteria supported by slides 1–2 and 9: SQL client/server relations, shared access, remaining design responsibilities, engine role, InnoDB-specific transactions/foreign keys/recovery, and row-lock contention. Learner does not generalize those guarantees to other engines.

All eight criteria taught by slides 3–4: types/keys/null constraints, enforced CHECK and references, version/mode verification, workflow limits, explicit atomic grouping versus autocommit, declared invariants/isolation, configured redo durability and external HTTP boundary. Quotes entail the actual learner reasoning.

All eight criteria supported by slides 5–6. Learner chooses the taught locking-read alternative, checking stock only after acquiring the lock and rejecting unavailable stock; this is transfer of the protected check/change rule, not prior-knowledge credit. It correctly distinguishes snapshots/current operations, retries whole deadlock-aborted transactions, explains clustered/secondary key cost and qualifies measured access paths and scans.

All eight criteria supported by slides 7–8 and diagrams: source/binlog/receive/apply lag, asynchronous loss, receipt not visibility, read policy and exclusive-authority promotion/routing, crash recovery versus failover/history, copied deletes, compatible base plus continuous logs/stopping point, and tested usable recovery. Learner correctly avoids inventing a fencing procedure.

All four criteria satisfied by the actual learner using slides 2–9: engine/schema fit, explicit concurrency/index choices and retries, delay-tolerant replicas without write-scaling promises and bounded connections, plus missing traffic/freshness/loss/latency/downtime requirements and tested recovery. Suitability is appropriately provisional.

sourceChecks.claim: Opened and inspected MySQL client/server description and relational role. Diagram correctly places application and server in distinct processes for this deployment model.
Opened InnoDB introduction: default engine, ACID DML, row-level locks, foreign keys and crash recovery confirmed; alternative-engine scope is explicit.

Opened SQL-mode example verifying abc-to-INT error versus warning/0. Keys/nulls checked at https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/create-table.html and CHECK true/unknown/enforcement at https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/create-table-check-constraints.html.

Opened COMMIT/ROLLBACK and default autocommit semantics. Default redo flushing and relaxed-setting loss checked at https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-parameters.html#sysvar_innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit. Database boundary does not include HTTP effects.

Opened isolation-level page: first consistent-read snapshot and different locking/range behavior. Current-data protection checked at https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-locking-reads.html; transaction retry/short duration at https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-deadlocks-handling.html.

Opened clustered/secondary index page: primary-key row storage and repeated key size confirmed. Plan inspection additionally checked at https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/using-explain.html. Diagram correctly allows covering-index lookup to omit full-row access.

Opened replication overview: default asynchronous source/replicas. Separate receive/apply verified at https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/replication-threads.html; candidate progress, client redirection and changed source role checked at https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/replication-solutions-switch.html. No automatic lossless failover claimed.

Opened PITR overview and https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/point-in-time-recovery-binlog.html: full base and subsequent binary logs support chosen-point recovery. Diagram requires both backup and later logs; restore testing is an operational validation requirement, not an asserted benchmark.

Opened InnoDB introduction; final choice synthesizes inspected engine, isolation, index and recovery sources. Benefits do not remove service/connection/transaction/recovery management, and no arbitrary capacity claim is made.
